---
title: "Getting started with zupix"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zupix)
f <- system.file("extdata", "gradient.png", package = "zupix")
```

zupix decodes PNG, JPEG, WebP and QOI, and encodes the same four, with every
codec compiled into the package. This article goes through the shapes it
reads into, the metadata it reports, the writers, the limits that guard
against hostile files, the C interface for other packages, how fast it is,
and where its output differs from the reference decoders.

## Three shapes

`pix_read()` returns one of three shapes, chosen with `as`.

A `nativeRaster` (the default) is 8-bit RGBA packed one pixel per integer,
as `png::readPNG(native = TRUE)` returns it. It is the smallest shape and
draws directly with `grid::grid.raster()` or `graphics::rasterImage()`.

```{r}
native <- pix_read(f)
class(native)
dim(native)
```

A double array holds values in `[0, 1]`, as `png::readPNG()` returns them:
`height x width x channels`, or a matrix for a grey image.

```{r}
dbl <- pix_read(f, as = "double")
dim(dbl)
range(dbl)
```

An integer array holds the sample values themselves, with their depth in a
`bits` attribute: `0..255` at 8 bits, `0..65535` at 16.

```{r}
int <- pix_read(f, as = "integer")
attr(int, "bits")
```

`bits` forces a depth, and `channels` adds channels: grey becomes RGB, and an
opaque alpha can be added. Removing a channel is refused, because turning
colour into grey or dropping transparency is a colour decision zupix leaves
to you.

```{r, error = TRUE}
dim(pix_read(f, as = "integer", channels = 4L))
attr(pix_read(f, as = "integer", bits = 16L), "bits")
pix_read(f, as = "integer", channels = 1L)
```

## Metadata

`pix_info()` reads an image's header and metadata without decoding pixels:
format, size, depth, colour type, transparency, interlacing, animation,
density, EXIF orientation, PNG's colour chunks, and whether an ICC profile
or EXIF data is present. It takes any number of paths and returns a row for
each.

```{r}
pix_info(f)
```

`pix_icc()` and `pix_exif()` return the ICC profile and the EXIF block as
raw vectors, or `NULL`. zupix never applies a profile: pass it to a
colour-management package.

The EXIF orientation says how a camera was held. Pixels come back as
stored; `pix_read(orient = TRUE)` or `pix_orient()` rotates or flips them
losslessly.

```{r}
small <- int[1:2, 1:3, 1]
small
pix_orient(small, 6L) # 90 degrees clockwise
```

Animated PNG and WebP decode their first frame, with an `animated`
attribute set to `TRUE`.

## Writing

`pix_write()` picks the format from the file's extension. Each format also
has its own writer with its own options.

```{r}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
pix_write(int, out, lossless = TRUE)
identical(pix_read(out, as = "integer"), int)
```

* `pix_write_png()` writes 8 or 16 bits with 1 to 4 channels, at a zlib
  `compression` from 0 to 9, with an optional ICC profile, EXIF block or
  sRGB rendering intent.
* `pix_write_jpeg()` takes a `quality` on libjpeg's scale, a chroma
  `subsampling` and `progressive`. JPEG stores no alpha: an alpha channel
  is dropped only when every pixel is opaque.
* `pix_write_webp()` is lossy or `lossless`, with a `method` trading speed
  for size.
* `pix_write_qoi()` writes 8-bit RGB or RGBA.

The writers take every shape `pix_read()` returns. Doubles are clamped to
`[0, 1]` and rounded; an integer array without a `bits` attribute is
treated as 8-bit if every value is at most 255. Without a `file`, the
writers return the encoded bytes as a raw vector.

```{r}
png <- pix_write_png(int, icc = as.raw(1:100))
length(png)
identical(pix_icc(png), as.raw(1:100))
```

## Limits and errors

A small file can declare a huge image. zupix parses the header, checks it
against `pix_limits()`, and allocates only then. The limits are the largest
side, the number of pixels, the bytes one decode may use, and the bytes of
metadata.

```{r}
pix_limits()
```

Every error is a condition of class `zupix_error` with one more specific
class, such as `zupix_limit_error`, `zupix_decode_error` (a corrupt or
truncated file; zupix never returns a partial image) or
`zupix_unsupported_error` (a valid feature outside zupix's scope, such as
12-bit or arithmetic-coded JPEG). Handle them by class; `?zupix-conditions`
lists them all.

```{r}
truncated <- readBin(f, "raw", 100)
tryCatch(
  pix_read(truncated),
  zupix_decode_error = function(e) "corrupt or truncated"
)
```

## From C

Other packages can call the same codecs from C, without going through R.
Declare `Imports: zupix` and `LinkingTo: zupix`, import any function of
zupix in your `NAMESPACE` so its DLL is loaded first, and include
`zupix-r.h`:

```c
#include <zupix-r.h>

SEXP my_image_width(SEXP bytes) {
  const zupix_api_v1 *api = zupix_api();
  zpx_info info = {sizeof info};
  if (api == NULL) Rf_error("zupix speaks another ABI version");
  if (api->probe(RAW(bytes), XLENGTH(bytes), NULL, &info) != ZPX_OK)
    return Rf_ScalarInteger(NA_INTEGER);
  return Rf_ScalarInteger((int) info.width);
}
```

The table also decodes into five pixel layouts with any row stride, extracts
ICC and EXIF data, and encodes all four formats through a callback.
Nothing in it calls R or raises an R error. Looking the table up does: if
zupix is not loaded, the first `zupix_api()` raises an R error, so make that
call from a `.Call` entry point, as above. `inst/include/zupix.h` documents
every function.

## Speed

Measured on a 12-megapixel synthetic photograph (R 4.5.2, macOS, x86_64),
against the packages that link the same formats' system libraries. Times
are medians; lower is faster.

| Operation | Reference | zupix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PNG decode to `nativeRaster` | `png` 0.19 s | 0.22 s |
| JPEG decode to `nativeRaster` | `jpeg` 0.18 s | 0.06 s |
| WebP decode | `webp` 2.52 s (doubles) | 0.25 s (`nativeRaster`) |
| PNG encode, level 6 | `png` 2.25 s | 2.82 s, same size |
| JPEG encode, quality 90 | `jpeg` 0.57 s | 0.86 s |
| WebP encode, quality 75 | `webp` 1.84 s | 1.52 s |
| `pix_info()` on 1,000 files | | 0.18 s |

PNG decoding spends about the same time in the decoder as libpng; the rest
is reading the whole file into memory first. zupix's JPEG decoder is
Wuffs, and its JPEG encoder is libjpeg-turbo without SIMD.

## Where zupix differs from the reference decoders

zupix is tested against reference decoders on public test suites. It
decodes every valid PngSuite image exactly as the png package does, and
every JPEG it was tested on exactly as libjpeg-turbo does. The jpeg package
bundles IJG libjpeg 9e, which upsamples colour differently, so colour JPEGs
read with it differ from zupix's by a few levels near sharp edges.

One difference comes from the version of Wuffs zupix bundles
(v0.4.0-alpha.12): on 8 of the 131 files in libwebp's test suite, lossy
WebP colour decodes up to 32 levels away from libwebp's output, though lossy
WebP is specified to decode exactly. Alpha, and lossless WebP, are exact.
The tests pin these files, so an update of Wuffs that fixes them shows up.

QOI decodes through the format's reference decoder, qoi.h, and matches it
exactly on every QOI test image.
